sentence_text: Should College Athletes Be Paid?
Do you think college athletes should be paid?
Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?
What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?
In my opinion, we should absolutely pay college athletes.
Why on earth shouldn't they be compensated for what they are doing for the school?
The truth is that the entire system of college sports is built on exploitation that is connected to a broader exploitative system.
The universities profit greatly from these athletes who, in many cases, are putting their health on the line.
There is also the possibility that young people are sustaining long-term damage from participating in sports.
Some might point out that some of these athletes are receiving scholarships in return for playing and therefore getting a free education.
This argument only highlights the broader exploitation at play.
College tuitions themselves are greatly inflated in the US.
The revenue that the schools are accruing from these young athletes is far greater that any loss from the exorbitant tuition fees.
And even when you allow that these students are getting a free education, why should it be at the expense of some other young person?
We put an emphasis on skills on the field when that player may have taken the place of an aspiring scientist.
In summary if the schools must be allowed to exploit young athletes in this way they should, at the very least, pay them for their efforts.
Is Listening to a Book Just as Good as Reading It?
Do you listen to audiobooks?
What are the benefits, in your opinion, of listening instead of reading?
Are there advantages to reading that cannot be gained by listening?
Which method do you prefer?
Why?
In my opinion, reading is always better than listening.
Reading involves a ritual that you do not get with an audiobook.
You sit down with a cup of coffee in a chair.
You open the book and hold it in your hands.
You flip pages and go at your own speed.
You are fully immersed in the author's words.
Nothing else is going on in the world.
It's an experience that is very unique.
With an audiobook you get none of that.
You hear the same story but you don't get the same experience.
With an audiobook, you get distracted.
You often times are doing other things at the same time.
You might end up missing part of the story because of that.
Reading takes time but it's so worth the time you spend to just sit there and enjoy reading.
You won't be able to multitask but that is part of the charm.
It's an old fashioned luxury you could say.
I think it's important to enjoy the experience of reading.
The experience of doing it, not just the actual task of hearing it like in an audio book.
While audiobooks do have their advantages, it's nice to disconnect from technology.
It even comes down to physically going to the library to get a book.
Rather than downloading an audiobook, it's so refreshing to visit a library.
That's another experience that you miss out on otherwise.
Obviously, audiobooks aren't going anywhere anytime soon but it's nice to detach from that world for awhile.
I firmly believe a physical book is better.
It feels nicer and I have better interactions with an actual book.
I'm all for the occasional audiobook sometimes.
It gives you a chance to take in a book when you are busy.
Nothing will ever beat a good old fashioned book and a cup of coffee on the weekend though.
How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, we should embrace the benefits of our digital devices.
The benefits of screen time are many.

In terms of education for our children, the use of computers and zoom and programming geared towards kids was the only thing for many schools that allowed them to teach at all the 2020-2021 school year.
Without technology and computer use, millions of children would have had absolutely no way to be in contact with their teachers and get even a semblance of learning.
The use of zoom classroom allowed teachers to visually see their students and for the kids in the classes to interact with their educator and each other.
Another advantage, speaking again in terms of children, that I have noticed is when my kids are playing multiplayer games online.
The ones I am most familiar with are Roblox and Overwatch.
My children have made friends from all around the world while playing these games.

One always has to be vigilant for online predators, and to educate children about being safe online, but the knowledge of other cultures and other countries my children have gained with communicating with youngsters from varied areas is immeasurable.
For youth to be able to interact with diverse people in a situation where you have to help each other to survive, can't really be taught in life outside a gaming situation.
have also noticed that my children are much more comfortable with technology than I was at their agee.
I could barely figure out how to turn a computer on when I was 12, let alone program or do research.
I have to ask my 12 year old for help with word sometimes, and my older teen with power point.
With the world and employment becoming increasingly digital and online, it is beneficial beyond words for children to know how to interact and use technology to their advantage.
I also believe that the benefits of screen time are not just for children.
These are just the advantages I am most tuned in to since I interact and see my children using their devices daily.
There may be some disadvantages, if you allow excess screen time or don't teach your child simple online safety rules, but the benefits simply outweigh the risks.
I am not advocating for a screen free life.
As with anything in this life, moderation and discipline are key.
This actually another benefit.
Teaching children how to limit their time, and how to apply restraints to online use can also teach structure and scheduling and organization to youth before they get out into the 'real world.'
The advantages are obvious to me and technology should be embraced and utilized as the tool it is.

Your entire life, you've been told you're deathly allergic to bees.
You've always had people protecting you from them, be it your mother or a hired hand.
Today, one slips through and lands on your shoulder.
You hear a tiny voice say 'Your Majesty, what are your orders?'
You look up and see the bee flitting about in front of you.
You're not sure what to say, since bees stress you out so much that it's hard to think.
The bee's wings are fluttering in an anxious manner.
This makes you feel nervous, because you know that bees are very sensitive to their surroundings.
Aren't they like dogs?
Dogs can sense anxiety and fear and when they sense that, this is when they start biting.
So if this bee senses that you're nervous, it might sting you.
You try to calm yourself down, but it's hard.
You ask the bee why he's approached you, and he says that he's been sent by the queen to give you a message.
'What's the message?'
you ask.
The bee tells you that the queen wants to know if you'd like to have a picnic with her.
'Why would I have a picnic with the queen?'
The bee says that he's really been sent to be your personal butler and that the invitation to picnic with the queen is a rare opportunity, not to be taken lightly.
'I don't know,' you say.
'After all, I'm deathly allergic to bees.'
The bee says that he's been specially trained to be gentle and that he'll be sure to keep his stinger tucked away.
And he promises that the queen doesn't want anything bad to happen to you either, so she'll be sure not to sting you too.
He also promises that the picnic food will be delicious, including all your favorite foods with a special treat at the end.
You agree.
After all, what is there to lose?
You love picnic food, and you're promised a spread that includes all your favorites, which include fried chicken, egg salad sandwiches, macaroni salad, potato salad, and chocolate cake.
So off you go with your butler bee to find the queen.
When you do, you're intrigued because she looks like a normal bee, but she's wearing a crown.
She's also wearing a long, flowing dress, and she's sitting on a blanket that's spread out over a field of flowers.
You sit down next to her, and she hands you a plate of fried chicken.
You're surprised because you didn't know that bees could cook, but this chicken is really good.
It's crispy on the outside and juicy on the inside.
You eat two pieces and then you ask for a sandwich.
The queen hands you an egg salad sandwich, which you eat.
Then you ask for a macaroni salad, and the queen hands you a bowl of that.
You eat it, and then you ask for a potato salad.
The queen hands you a bowl of that, and you eat it.
You're about to ask for chocolate cake, but you stop yourself.
You're so full you could almost burst.
The queen laughs.
She finds you humorous.
'Why did you bring me here?'
you ask.
The queen smiles.
'I wanted to show you my kingdom,' she says.
She tells you that she noticed that you have decided to plant a garden recently in your backyard.
However, you've sprayed a bunch of insecticide everywhere, and that is very concerning to her since some of her bees in her kingdom have gotten sick or died after flitting over to your garden.
She wants you to stop using the insecticide.
'But I'm allergic to most bugs and bees, and thus I need to keep them at bay,' you tell her.
'No,' she says.
'I'm giving my personal orders to my kingdom that no bee shall sting you ever, as long as you get rid of the insecticide.'
You think about this offer and decide to take the queen up on it.
After all, you don't want to be stung, and she's pretty nice.
She's even treated you to a delicious picnic.
So you agree to stop using the insecticide.
The queen is happy with this arrangement and tells you that she'll be sure to send her butler bee to you every now and then to check up on you.
She tells you that if you ever need anything from her kingdom, you should just let your butler bee know.
You tell her that you'll do just that!

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, it's a free country so one is free to do whatever they so choose, so long as it's legal.
And I've never heard of any laws against mountain climbing, snowboarding, or any other adventure sport.
In fact, I just read up on some laws lately and I didn't see any that forbade such activities.
And I should know a good bit about the law, because I'm a law student at the University of Nevada, Reno.
That said, mountain climbers, snowboarders and pretty much anybody who's into the extreme sports scene has to be aware of one thing: they're not invulnerable.
And the more extreme the sport, the more likely there will be accidents and injuries.
But as long as the athletes themselves are aware of the risks, there's no reason why they shouldn't engage in such activities.
After all, isn't living life to the fullest what being alive is all about?
And don't we all take calculated risks, even for some very dangerous activities, like speeding on the freeway or crossing the street without looking one hundred percent both ways?
One could even say that extreme mountain climbing is much safer than riding an inner city school bus!
I mean, I get why that's a hyperbole but you know what I mean.
It's an individual's decision to risk his or her life; strict liability is what tort professors always say.
And the same goes for the parents of extreme sports enthusiasts.
My parents never discouraged me from snowy excursions because they knew I was capable of making my own choices, and it's really none of their business anyways.
I was admittedly fortunate that I never got hurt very badly; I broke my nose once, but nothing major.
My tort professor would be proud of my astute choice of body parts to be injured by!
In law school, they teach us that if you're aware of the risk, you're considered to have consented to it.
I don't really think anyone in the U.S. really wants to live in a country where the state is paternalistic enough to put the kibosh on our hobbies, but I digress.
I mean, look at the amount of people who start smoking, despite the government's strong anti-smoking campaigns.
The bottom line is that people should do whatever they want as long as they don't infringe on anybody else's rights.
And I don't see how one can infringe on anyone else's rights by doing extreme sports.
I suppose if one injured another's property somehow, they could be in court, but that's a different story.

In the alternative, I suppose one could argue that extreme sports are not productive, but this is hardly an argument against extreme sports; I mean everybody does things that aren't necessarily productive.
I just don't think that the inherent danger of extreme sports justifies their prohibition.
It's not reasonable to prohibit them because they're too dangerous.
It's much easier to prohibit dangerous things that could adversely affect innocent others, like drunk driving.
But here, it's just the athlete hurting himself.
So in conclusion, I think that extreme sports enthusiasts should be entitled to pursue their hobby without fear of persecution based on the inherent risk present in such participation.
But let it be clear that I am not supporting anything that violates any laws, of which I am aware no such laws exist.
And of course, safety measures should be taken, because there are still risks to be aware of.
And I'm quite sure my tort professor would be proud of my argument against the conclusions of social activists who think extreme sports are too dangerous.
They can stay home in their granny panties.
I'm going to go check my snowboarding blog now.

Athletes give up a great deal of their time and freedom to appease the irrational exuberance of fanatical, undereducated audiences.

They probably joined the college football team just to be on a sports team.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, we should be both worried about excessive screen time, but also glad that the pandemic did not hit so early that we would be denied the chance to use our screens in this fashion.
I am worried about screen time bin general, not just during the pandemic, ecause I believe that it is a major factor in the epidemic of childhood obesity and the rise in childhood diabetes.
This is, of course, also a factor of portion sizes and the increasing amounts of sugar and fat that are included in convenience foods that are marketed toward children.
Given that most families have two working parents, and some of them have more than one job, we cannot pass judgment on families for this outcome.
They simply do not have the time to cook at home or to engage in vigorous exercise with their children.

If screens were not so enticing to children (perhaps, because we lived in an earlier time) or because parents were deliberately denying their children screen time, then it is possible that they would play outside more often.
This additional exercise would be good for their bodies and possibly their minds as well.
I am also worried about screen time because of the potential for addiction.
Video games and social media are almost tailor-made to feed out brain's desire for feedback and stimulation, and it can be hard to drag ourselves away from devices that give us what we want.
Although these trends are worrying, we have to accept the world as it is, and there is little that we can do to change other people's behavior unless they themselves are willing to change.
This would require a mutual desire in both children and parents to limit their exposure to screens, and this perfect situation is rare.
My broader point is that we should be worried about screen time, especially for children.
We should also be worried about the amount of time that we spend on our own screens, and we should try to limit our screen time as much as possible.
Social media and even video games can have the same effect on adult brains as they do on children.
Likewise, a sedentary lifestyle can be unhealthy for anyone, so we need to force ourselves to get up and move, preferably outside.
When it comes to the pandemic, however, I think we have to accept that screens (while dangerous when over-used) are very helpful.
We need to be able to communicate with our families and friends, and we need to be able to access information about the virus.
Internet-connected devices may feed our addictions, but they also allow us to keep in touch with the people we care about.
If kids were playing outside with their friends, they might have spread the virus and caused much more loss of life than we have already seen.
And keeping kids indoors, in isolation, without any way to communicate would probably be worse for their long-term health than excessive socialization on the internet has been.
And so, te bottom line is that we should be worried about screen time, but we should also be glad that the pandemic hit when it did.
Screentime has been a crutch that has helped get us through a very difficult period in our lives and in our history.
However, whenever we are safely able to do so, we should try to return to a life in which interactions are sometimes made in person, and in which people interact in the real world.
It is healthier for us on so many levels to be active, social, and connected.
Once the acute risk of disease has passed, or has at least been controlled, we should try to get ourselves back out there.

ot only that, but when they are not there for them anymore, people in loved ones lives may slowly start to fade away as well.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, the question of whether some sports are too dangerous to be called a sport is really one about degree.
How dangerous are they?
There's something that is dangerous but widely accepted such as school sports.
Even though you might break a bone (or fracture something), we know that statistically we'll be ok. Then there's more extreme sports such as base jumping, mountain climbing and wingsuit flying.
Those are the other end of the spectrum.
There, we know that there is a non-zero chance we will die.
There's always the possibility.
So if we divide sports into somewhat dangerous and very dangerous, then we can start to look at if it is selfish to participate.
We might think that if someone dies doing something, they brought it on themselves.
Especially if it is an extreme sport.
There's people who have died going over Niagra Falls in a barrel.
I think we'd all agree that didn't serve some greater purpose.
However there are people who go mountain climbing not for glory, but as a challenge to themselves.
It's a personal goal.
Is that selfish?
It's hard to say.
Then there's people who do these things to make money.
Some people make money filming themselves hanging from famous landmarks or parachuting from them.
Again, is that selfish?
They are doing it to make money for themselves or their family.
I think that only extreme sports could be considered selfish and that's still debatable.
It's also important to consider why people do these things.
Everyone has a reason that maybe we don't understand.
Maybe it's to support their family.
Maybe it's to try and grow as a person by achieving a goal.
Maybe they're just suicidal and think even the small chance of death is worth it.
There's countless reasons so it's hard to broadly judge someone or to call them selfish.
This is a free country and we're allowed to do what we want.
People may say its selfish but that doesn't mean it actually is.
We just have our opinions at the end of the day, right or wrong.

he benefits of screen time are many and include: cnnecting with family and friends, while at the same time, reducing the risk of transmitting the virus; staying informed about the latest news and developments; and managing our work, and bills, from the comfort of home.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, the amount of danger involved in a sport should have no bearing on whether that activity constitutes a sport or not.
A sport is defined to be a physical activity that is governed by a set of rules or customs and often engaged in competitively.
Nowhere in the definition of a sport does it say that the activity must be safe.
I'm pretty sure if I were to look up this definition in the dictionary the dictionary would be silent on safety.
And in fact, think about some of the most popular sports in America.
Football, hockey, boxing and mixed martial arts are all extremely dangerous sports.
I recently read that football players are three times more likely to die from a brain injury than the average person.
And don't even get me started on the dangers involved in boxing and mixed martial arts.
Did you know that in the past decade, there have been over 1,000 deaths in boxing?
And further, that there have been over 1,000 deaths in mixed martial arts since the sport's inception in 1993?
If we have those kinds of statistics for sports that are considered to be 'safe,' what does that say about the dangers involved in other sports?
I just don't think that there is any way to make a sport that is inherently competitive and inherently involves a test of physical and mental strength totally safe from all risks.
After all, think about some of the sports that you'd likely to be consider more mundane and safe.
Let's take golf, for example.
Did you know that there are over 100 deaths per year from golf-related accidents?
Yes, that's right.
Those deaths are the result of golfers falling off of golf carts, being hit by golf balls and even dying from heart attacks.
Some golfers also get arthritis because of the repetitive swinging of the golf club.
And then let's consider cross country.
I've heard of runners getting heat stroke and even dying from it.
And as a former runner, I can tell you that running is not a safe sport.
Many of my teammates suffered from shin splints, stress fractures and even plantar fasciitis.
And plenty of my teammates also had to deal with knee and ankle injuries.
On top of that, cross country is a sport where you can get hit by a car.
Many of my teammates also had psychological issues involved with the sport too, because of the pressure to perform well and to break school records.
As a result, many of the athletes developed eating disorders and even had to seek psychological counseling.
So is extreme mountain climbing really that much more dangerous than the sports that we all know and love to be safe sports?
I don't really think so.
While it's true that extreme mountain climbing is dangerous, it's also true that there are plenty of other sports that are just as dangerous.
On the surface, it might seem that extreme mountain climbing is more dangerous than other sports, but when you really look at the statistics, it's not that much different.
And extreme mountain climbing deaths and injuries might be more publicized because of the nature of the sport, but that doesn't mean that it's any more dangerous than other sports.
When was the last time you heard about a golfer dying from a heart attack or a runner dying from heat stroke?
It's likely that those stories haven't made the headlines but that doesn't necessarily indicate that those sports are any safer than extreme mountain climbing.
So in conclusion, I think that it's silly to say that extreme mountain climbing is a dangerous sport.
All sports are dangerous so it's sort of just a redundancy to have to expressly state that.
And I think that it's also silly to say that extreme mountain climbing is not a sport.
Does it involve physical activity?
Does it involve a set of rules?
Does it involve competition?
I can check all of those boxes.
So it certainly meets the criteria for a sport.
I think we can all set aside the level of safety for the sake of argument here, because it's not really that relevant to the question of whether or not extreme mountain climbing is a sport.
In conclusion, I'm someone who enjoys a good debate.
So I'm willing to listen to your arguments and to consider your point of view.
But that doesn't mean that I'm going to change my mind.
I'm very certain that extreme mountain climbing is a sport and I'm also very certain that it's not any more dangerous than other sports.
But I welcome you to share your thoughts on the matter.

How Do You Think Technology Affects Dating?

Have you ever used dating apps?
If so, what has it been like for you?
If not, why not?
How do you think technology -- like apps, Netflix, social media and texting -- affects dating and relationships?
In your opinion, does it improve or worsen romantic interactions?
How so?
In my opinion, technology has made dating and relationships better.
In the past, in order to meet the 'right person' you have to be almost preternaturally lucky.
A chance invitation, lucky coincidence, and happenstance ruled the day.
For every million compatible partners, you'd be lucky to meet one.
Now, with the advent of dating apps and social media, you can find compatible people in your area with a few clicks.
And there's no rule you can't go out of your area.
I have met people who have travelled thousands of miles to meet someone they thought might be the right one.
Technology has aade it easier to communicate.
But this ease of communication comes with a cost.
It's easy to send a message, but it's hard to know if the other person is interested.
It's easier to lie.
It is easier to be too casual about relationships.
In the feed of potential partner after potential partner, faces can become a blur.
Partners can be more interchangeable.
The phrase 'there are more fish in the sea' has never been more true.
Technology has also made it easier to cheat.
There is precious little independent verification, in most dating apps, of the personal details and photos posted by members.
Is the photo accurate?
Was it taken in the last year?
Is it even a photo of the person who posted it?
Are the personal details even remotely accurate?
In real life, maybe 15% of the people you meet are fit and trim.
On the apps, its 90% if not more!
echnology has also made it easier to be a 'player''.
And that is not a good thing.
I think dating apps are a mixed bag.
If used with caution and a healthy skepticism, they definitely improve the chance of a solid match.
But used frivolously, they can be an entry into a world of pain and miscommunication.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, there should be a balance of emotional, social and physical interaction online as well as offline.
I don't think it's necessary to go full Luddite on the Internet, saying we should do away with Facebook and mobile devices.
Some parents are considering this for their families, but it could lead to isolation, loneliness and even depression for kids, who are using social media to stay connected with their friends.
Frankly, that's totally counterproductive.
At the same time, we can't squander our digital lives on mindless games and social media, which the research shows is the main reason too many of us spend too much time on the Internet.
And there are plenty of people who would be better off unplugging completely.

For example, some people get sucked into their digital lives to such a degree that they lose out on things we may now take for granted--a night out with friends, time for relaxation and unwinding, reading a good book, heck, even going on vacation.
While our screens are addicting, there's nothing inherently wrong with using them in the right way.
And, indeed, for some people, the Internet can be a real lifeline.
For example, a recent scientific study shows that a slight increase in Facebook use can actually be a good thing for people with disabilities--if it's used in a healthy manner.
This is because this social network lets people with disabilities communicate with others who are similar, at a time when they might otherwise feel alone in their social world.
I have a friend named Soeurette, who was born with cerebral palsy.
Soeurette uses Facebook to communicate with other people in her situation--something she wouldn't be able to do if social media doesn't exist.
Soeurette always says  'Thank God for Facebook,' because, without it, she would feel a little more alone in a world of able-bodied people.
So I'm always mindful of her viewpoint and that it's perfectly OK to balance screen time with face-to-face, real-world interactions.
My niece, Everly, is a great example of how that balance can work.
Everly is a typical nine-year-old girl, with an Internet-savvy iPhone and an iPad 2.
She usually spends a little time on each of these gadgets each day.
Her favorite apps are games, which are understandably popular with kids her age.
But a recent study shows that Everly's screen time is still well within recommended limits.
She hasn't forgotten how to play with dolls, act out stories or read books.
In other words, she balances her time between the 'real' world and the digital one--and that's a good thing.
So what's the best way to achieve a healthy balance?
With my kids, we've found that we need to start with a chat about how we can be better digital citizens.
I always tell my daughter Harper that being a good citizen of the Internet means that she should use her technology responsibly.
It also means that she shouldn't spend too much time on her devices--not because technology or the Internet are bad, but because life is about more than just Facebook.
Harper and her brother, Bryson, get it; they know that many things in life--and especially life online--are about balance.
That's why our family doesn't have hard limits on Internet usage, but still encourages smart use of technology--such as putting away devices for dinner.
And on weekends, we always allow some unplugged time for family fun, be it on the golf course or playing sports.
Oftentimes, we'll grill together for supper, just the four of us.
Everly loves grilling with her dad, because it's a shared family-time experience.
And Bryson just enjoys eating the boneless buffalo wings I make for him, which are as big as his head.
So there's the balance I was talking about earlier--social time with family, physical recreation, even a little bit of time spent cooking.
In conclusion, I don't think we need to be too concerned about screen time, as long as we're using it in moderation.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, athletes should be permitted to engage in any sport they choose as long as they are educated about the risks involved and choose to take those risks upon themselves.

The reason I believe this, is that existing sports already contain some inherently dangerous components, most of which result in serious injury on a fairly frequent basis, and some of which can even result in death.
For example, football players experience bodily collisions with other players to the point of severe bodily damage on a regular basis.
Broken bones and torn ligaments are almost routine, and concussions are common.

A fair amount of football players --particularly in the high school and college ranks--suffer from post-concussion syndrome (which may not present itself for several months after the injury), and can effect them for the rest of their lives, and several players have suffered neck injuries that have resulted in permanent paralysis.

Boxing, of course, is another sport that has a decidedly high risk of injury and death, as does MMA, while even sports that don't involve hard impacts with other players, like baseball and tennis, have their own unusual dangers, such as flying balls and obstacles that result in serious injury, and track competitors risk sprains or broken limbs from hurdles, high jumps and the long jump.

Even golfers , whose sport is considered relatively safe in the grand scheme of things, can suffer minor injuries like chronic arthritis from repetitive motion, and serious injuries and even death by lightning strikes.
My point is, that the risks of engaging in sports, are already high, and are inherent, and expected.

Perhaps sports that mean certain death should be banned, but barring that, I can't see preventing competition in extreme sports, because if that were to occur, many just as dangerous (or even more so) existing sports would need to be banned as well,  which would lead to very few sports in which an athlete could lawfully compete.

What Are the Most Important Things Students Should Learn in School?

What is the most important thing you have learned in school?
How has this knowledge affected your life?
How do you think it will help your success in the future?
In my opinion, students should learn primarily the basics of reading, writing, and arithmetic, in addition to a foundation of understanding in history, science, and the arts.
These things have long been considered the basics of a good education, and I believe they should remain so.
A student who can't read will have difficulty learning any other subject, inside of school, or out, and a student who can't write will have difficulty communicating with others.

The fundamentals of math are necessary for students to do things like balance a checkbook,  figure out how much change they should get back from a cashier, budget household expenses as an adult, and do many other things that are necessary for everyday life.
Eventually they'll need an understanding of math, as working adults, to not be reliant on accountants to do their taxes.
Students need to understand world history , as well as the history of their own country, in order to understand how the world came to be the way it is today.

They need to understand the basics of science in order to understand how the world works, and how to use that knowledge to their advantage, such as by understanding how to use a computer, or how to fix a car.
Some knowledge of the arts is needed in order for students to appreciate the beauty of the world around them, and to be able to enjoy life.
Of course, there are many other things that students need to know.
They need to know how to interact with others, how to be a good citizen, and how to be a good person.
They need skills that will help them be successful in life, such as how to interact with others, how to be a good employee and how to take care of themselves.
They need to learn job skills.
These things are not really the job of the public school system, though.
They are the job of the parents, society at large, colleges, and vocational schools.
The public schools try to do too much already.
They should instead focus on the basics, and leave the rest to other institutions, and endeavor to provide children with a foundation upon which they can build their future.
If schools are able to construct this basic foundation, other institutions will be able to build upon that foundation, and the students will be better off for it, as will society as a whole.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, this could be considered selfish if a person has a family and children at home.
Whenever a person engages in an extreme sport, they are taking the danger and the risks that go with it.
It is possible that they could end up leaving their family behind if they are injured or worse on one of these daring adventures.
Although most people train hard for these experiences, not every scenario can be accounted for so a person could be left unprepared for many types of events.
It is very rare that these kinds of accidents happen, but they do happen.
While it is sometimes worth the risk to be happy, too much risk can come back to cause severe harm.

The consideration has to be, how much of the sport is ingrained into a person's happiness and if the person gives up the sport so that they can be sure to be there for their family, will the person become resentful and angry?
It is the hard decision to make, but one that has to be made.
Even though anything can happen at any time, there are activities that come with more risk than others.
Extreme sports seem to be one of those.
As much as a person does not want to admit this fact, their family might be the thing that makes sure they are always careful and never taking any unnecessary chances.
There are times when a person can think of the thrill that is felt on a mountain top or the one that is felt while doing a certain sport and nothing can really replace that feeling.
The trouble is that these sensations are so controlled by adrenaline and endorphins that it is only a fleeting feeling.
The feeling of wanting the thrill and adrenaline rush will continue to increase over time.
Eventually, the feelings of wanting that rush will outweigh the need for family and a feeling of being at home.
As a person's desire to pursue this thrill increases, their need for family decreases.
This type of situation needs to be anticipated prior to any lifetime commitments and conclusions and agreements need to be made.
A person might not even have to make that decision but it would be good for them to know what might happen if their focus does change.
This is a reminder for people to always have time for the family and not to focus all of their time on work or hobbies which eventually become so important.

Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?
In your opinion, are we being bad citizens if we don't keep up with the news?
Do you think all people have some responsibility to know what is going on in the world?
Does engaging with current events actually do anything at all?
Why do you think the way you do?
In my opinion, it depends on what the news tells us.
These days, the internet, the radio, the TV, and the newspapers are full of terrible news, unfortunately.
So it depends on what, if anything, we can do about this news.
I would argue that things such as COVID news are important to pay attention to, so that we can know what is safe to do and how we can protect others.
Other news can be very important, but also deeply distressing to read, and knowing the information doesn't actually allow us to help other people.
When it becomes important is when it comes to what we share, and how we participate civically.
There is so much misinformation out there, that we should be informed when we choose to share a fact or opinion.
That is the least we can do.
Plus, if we see a dubious-looking claim, it is up to us to get the correct information and correct the person.
Furthermore, when it comes time to go into a voting booth, we need to be filled with good, true information.
There are cases where we would be bad citizens if we aren't up to date on world happenings.
Especially if we're an undecided voter, or if there's a crisis unfolding where we can personally have a true impact.
Don't get me wrong, it's generally important to be up to date on what is happening in the world.
But for the sake of our own mental state, it can be helpful to filter what we take in.
Do we need to know the latest guidelines from the CDC?
Do we need to know the details of a presidential summit in Europe?
Less so.

Once again, this is good information to know, but there is so much news out there that we not only should not be expected to always be completely on top of it, but we also should feel free to not absorb every morsel of it.
People think that if they don't keep up with the news, then other people will think less of them.
But I think the issue lies more with making sure to get correct and complete information before forming an opinion, and living your life based upon truth.

As long as I have knowledgeable opinions based on objective facts, I will be able to participate in a democracy, I will be able to advocate for what I believe in, and I will be able to contribute to my society.
Another situation where it is indeed important to be up to date on the news is when it comes to having perspective.
Realizing where one stands in the world.

For example, recent news from Afghanistan should cause people to feel strong empathy for the people there, and recognize their privilege, if not there, to be living in a place that is not under Taliban rule.
One need not necessarily pore over every detail, but we should be informed enough to be compassionate.
In conclusion, we don't need every bit of news out there.
And we need to filter what we take in, making sure to only draw from reliable sources.
But we can also accept how overwhelming the 24-hour news cycle can be, and realize that we don't need to know every single thing that's happening.
We can still be well informed, without being exhausted.
Just make sure you always have a grip on reality, and are well informed on what matters for you to be a good citizen.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, all that time spent in front of a computer or phone screen, even if it is understandable under the circumstances,  is not good for us.
It is not good for our health, our relationships, or our ability to connect with the world around us.
In terms of health, staring at a screen can cause eye strain, dry eyes, headaches and neck pain.
Though people might attempt 'online exercise programs', screen time in general leads to more sedentary behavior, and therefore to weight gain and obesity.
It also creates trends in behavior that might carry on into the future, when the virus is no longer a concern, so these negative impacts on healthy behavior could be long-lasting.
When it comes to relationships, looking at other people via a screen is not the same as interacting with  them in person.
Particularly when it comes to children, there is a lot of research showing that the more time they spend on screens, the less time they spend interacting with their parents and siblings.
Certain social and behavioral cues can't be conveyed on a screen; the same is true of the non-verbal cues that are so important to communication.
While the impact on adults might be relatively minor, all this screen time is causing a generation of children to miss out on the important developmental benefits of face-to-face interaction.

In terms of general connection with the world around us, screen time is causing us to miss out on real things, occurring in our neighborhoods and communities, and focus on arbitrary things, occurring only on the internet.
or on the other side of the world.

In this way, screen time is causing us to lose a proper sense of place and connection with the world around us, and by that, I mean the portions of the world that should be important and meaningful to us.
Instead we're ending up with stronger connections to people we will never meet, places we will never visit, and things that don't really affect us.
The fact is, the dramatic increase in relying on computers and the internet to get by, was meant to be a temporary solution to a short-term problem.
It was never meant to be a permanent solution to a long-term problem, and if we treat it that way, we may find that the problems it causes, are far worse than anything caused by a novel flu virus.

In the past, meeting someone and starting to date them was mostly just a question of luck.
One had to be in the right place, at the right time, and had to be physically attractive enough to catch the eye of a passing stranger.

But now, more people can put themselves out there, and have many more opportunities to meet others.
IAnothertbig impact that echnology has had on dating is that it has made it easier to find people who share your interests.

In the past, you might meet an attractive stranger, start dating, and eventually realize that you have little or nothing in common.
This could lead to painful breakups in the worst case, and to wasted time in the best case.
Technology has saved us from both outcomes.

It was just a polite way to invite someone over for what you assume will be an intimate encounter.
Netflix has merely provided an opening that some people may mutually exploit.
In conclusion, I think that the future of dating will continue to be technology-focused, and I think that this is ultimately a good thing.

Should College Athletes Be Paid?
Do you think college athletes should be paid?
Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?
What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?
In my opinion, the opinion presented by McDavis is broadly appealing, but it ignores key facts about what is already happening in college sports.

Top universities are already paying for a select few athletes, but they are doing so with perks and special treatment that ultimately does not benefit those students in the same way that fair payment for service would.
The NCAA is a monopoly that has no incentive to change the way it operates., and sadly, there is practically a requirement that aspiring professional athletes must compete on the NCAA's terms.
It would be great if college sports could live up to the ideal of scholars who compete as a hobby and as a way to show pride in their universities, but this is clearly not the case in reality.
College is viewed as a stepping stone by a lucky few who feel that they have what it takes to make a career out of playing sports.
They are generally given special treatment by professors who view the sports teams as a vital part of the university's balance sheet, and often are not held to the same standards as other students.
And we should not judge the players themselves too harshly for this system, because they did not make the rules.
The NCAA and the colleges require them to work more than full time at their sport, all for the good of the school.
They do not have time to pursue a full-time education and to work to support themselves.
The NCAA's rules argainst paying these players ae designed to protect the interests of the universities and the NCAA itself, not the players.

This means that college sports attracts only those who have the financial wherewithal to attend college while essentially doing nothing but training and competing in sports, all for the hoped-for reward of a professional sports contract after graduation.
This is not what the college athletic ideal hoped for, and we should stop pretending that those ideals are being upheld.
If we accept reality, on the other hand, and pay athletes for their service, then they can pursue their education either part time or after they have competed to their own satisfaction.
As it currently stands, however, we are just forcing student athletes to work for their institutions for nothing more than a vague promise of future riches.
This is not fair, and it is not right.
No matter how you look at it, this is either a violation of labor laws, or it is a violation of the NCAA's stated ideal of the scholarly athlete.
Nobody can, and nobody should, accept the system in its current form.
Giving students housing allowances and other forms of compensation is just a disguised form of payment, so why do we pretend that a paycheck would change anything?
I contend that the college-athletics system has evolved, and that if people are happy with the way it is set up, then the employees who are keeping it going should be paid fairly for their efforts.
If any coaches or talent scouts disagree, then I would invite them to give up their salaries and instead work for the same promises that they give to their students.

I currently have a job working as a restaurant hostess.

For example, if a customer asks me a question, and I don't answer them quickly, it can make the customer angry.
As another example, if I answer the phone in a cheerful manner, it makes the customer happy.

These should really be the pillars of what students should learn in school.

Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?
In your opinion, are we being bad citizens if we don't keep up with the news?
Do you think all people have some responsibility to know what is going on in the world?
Does engaging with current events actually do anything at all?
Why do you think the way you do?
In my opinion, a democratic society should refrain from imposing any kind of duty on its citizens unless absolutely needed.
So, people do have a duty to support themselves, care for themselves and their family, and refrain from harming others or breaking the law, since those things are necessary for a society to function.
Following the news, however, is not, and should not be used as a measure of good or bad citizenship.
The question then becomes, is it even useful, or desirable to follow it?
I think it is useful, but not for the reasons most people do.
It is needed on a local level, to know what is going on in your community, and to be able to participate in local issues, and to respond in case of local emergencies.

On a national level, it is needed to know what is going on in your country that might directly affect you, like changes in the law, or larger natural disasters, or massive economic shifts, so that you can respond appropriately.
However, exploring political or social issues beyond this, or following the news for entertainment, is not useful, and can even be harmful.
The reasons for this are myriad.
First of all, the news is not objective, and is often deliberately misleading.

If a citizen wanted to know what was going on on a global level, it's not like they could just turn on the news and get a clear, unbiased picture of what is happening, so such a thing might not be practically attainable.
That being the case, following the news can suck up a lot of time, and time is a valuable resource, that might be better devoted to meeting one's actual obligations.
The news can also be very upsetting, and can cause unnecessary anxiety and stress.

It could be said that being a good citizen might be better served, by not following the news, and causing oneself stress, and wasting time, and that a good citizen should instead expend their effort on focusing on their own life, and the lives of those they are responsible for.

I'd say being well informed is a nice idea, and a good goal to strive for, but that it is not a duty, and that it is not something that should be used to judge a person's status as a citizen, but instead it is a personal choice, and a personal goal, that could be considered a luxury, pursued by and possibly attainable only by those citizens who have the time, money, and energy to do so, in a responsible manner.

What Stereotypical Characters Make You Cringe?

Would you ever not watch or read something because of its offensive portrayal of someone?
In my opinion, the most offensive stereotypes are the ones that are used to make a character seem less than human.

For instance, the idea that a person who is gay, or a person of color, or a woman, or an immigrant, or a person with disabilities is less of a person than someone who is straight, white, male, native-born and able-bodied.
Well known examples of this include the portrayal of the Native American as a savage, the portrayal of African Americans as lazy and stupid, the portrayal of women as weak and subservient to men.
Each of these examples is offensive because it dehumanizes a group of people.
So, in the sense that I'm a person with high moral standards about how to treat my fellow humans, I view all of these as 'cringe worthy.'
The question of whether I would avoid reading a book or watching a movie because of a stereotyped portrayal, is a more difficult one.
Is it possible for a work to be so well written that I can overlook the offensive portrayal?
I find it hard to believe that I could ever do that, but I suppose it's possible.
I think the problem is that I would have to be so caught up in the story that I wouldn't constantly notice the offensive portrayal.
Alternatively, the offensive portrayal could be a small enough part of the overall work that I could overlook it.
In either of these cases, the stereotype wouldn't be enough to make me stop reading or watching.
However, I find this unlikely.
For the most part, a work that is offensive in this way is offensive because the author or director is trying to be offensive.

So, the offensive portrayal is likely to be a large part of the work, or at least a large part of the author's or director's intent, and if the same stereotype doesn't occur constantly, other offensive stereotypes will.
Also, the use of stereotypes suggests a lack of creativity on the part of the author or director.
So, it's unlikely that the rest of the work will be so well written that the stereotype would be particularly easy to overlook.
We live in a world where the use of stereotypes is so common that it's hard to avoid them.
However, we also live in an era where people are becoming more aware of the harm that stereotypes cause.
In this day and age, it's not so easy to write off stereotypes as mere lazy writing.
It makes more sense to view them as a conscious choice to dehumanize people.
Perhaps rather than merely avoiding these works, we should be calling them out for what they are, and calling on the creators to cease using them, and treat people with the respect that they deserve.

In my opinion, we shouldn't really get too up in arms about screen time during COVID.
Yes, we do need to be aware of the possible side effects of excessive use of digital devices on our mental and physical health.

But we also need to be aware of the risks of staying disconnected from digital networks.
Especially in this time of fear and social distancing, we shouldn't be afraid to stay connected in a meaningful way.

And we all know that having someone who is there for you during a crisis can make all the difference.
Who cares if the call was made on a laptop, a smartphone or an old fashioned telephone?
I certainly don't, because it's the experience of connection, not the device itself, that matters most.

It has been the only way I feel I have been able to stay connected with my family and friends around the world.
My family lives in Thailand, and I work from home in London, so it's been a real lifeline for me to stay in touch with the people who mean the most in my life.

In my opinion, yes, schools absolutely should provide free pads and tampons.
I have experienced period poverty, and I certainly think that schools should be required to provide free pads and tampons.
It is a necessity that helps women survive a natural, biological process.

If a school can provide toilet paper, soap, Band-Aids, and other products with the intent of helping students be healthy and comfortable, they should be able to provide pad and tampons, which would help greatly with addressing period-related problems such as bleeding through clothes.
I have been caught in uncomfortable positions and circumstances before due to the fact that I didn't have enough pads and tampons with me, and it can be humiliating.
This is because I've gotten my period on days when I've been wearing clothes I didn't want to ruin or clothes that weren't made from material that could be easily washed.
For example, once I was wearing a borrowed dress when I got my period, and it was made out of satin.
I had borrowed it from a friend, and I didn't want to ruin her dress because it meant a lot to her.
During math class, I suddenly felt a warm and uncomfortable sensation under the skirt of my dress.
It was my period.
I was so grossed out because of the pressure of the blood, I went to the bathroom to clean myself up.
When I stood up, I realized that I bled through my panties and all down the back of my legs.
It gets worse.
I realized that I'd left a huge red stain on the bottom of my dress after going to the bathroom.
I tried to wash it off when no one was looking, but the blood completely stained the bottom of my dress.
I had no idea what to do.
And I was mortified because I realized that everyone in math class was probably able to see the big red stain on the back of my dress.
I kept wiping my behind to try to conceal the stain, but instead, it got worse.
That's because I'd only made the stain even bigger and more obvious.
Even worse, I still didn't have any pads or tampons on me, so I was forced to walk around school all day with blood on my backside and the bottom of my dress.
And the bloody spot kept getting bigger because my flow was so heavy on that day.
The shame I felt was terrible, and I should never have to feel that way simply because it's so hard for me to get pads and tampons.
The experience was so uncomfortable and humiliating, and I wish it hadn't happened to me.
That's why I believe that schools should be required to provide pads and tampons for students.
If during my horrible experience at school I'd had adequate amounts of pads and tampons, I probably could have fixed the problem quickly and discreetly.
I wouldn't have needed to walk around all day with blood on my behind and the bottom of my dress.
I could even tell that other students knew that I had my period, and they probably thought that I was gross and disgusting for bleeding through my clothes.
And quite frankly, I couldn't even blame them if that's what they thought.
If I were in their shoes, I would've thought that, too.
So in conclusion, schools absolutely should be providing pads and tampons in their restrooms for students, in my opinion.
There is just no difference between pads and tampons and toilet paper, soap, Band-Aids and other products that are already provided in schools.

Should Schools Provide Free Pads and Tampons?

Should schools step in to help?
Should schools be required to provide free pads and tampons to students?
How are pads and tampons similar to toilet paper, soap, Band-Aids and other products that are already provided in schools?
How are they different?
In my opinion, pads and tampons fall into a category of personal products that are both essential to students at times, but are generally only provided 'as needed.'
That is, they aren't provided as a matter of course.
Do schools supply students with enough toilet paper to use at home?
No.
Do they give students soap to take with them and wash their hands 7 days a week?
Heck no!
Are students given a supply of Band-Aids to take home and use whenever they cut themselves during the year?
Of course not!
All of these items are provided to students when they are needed on school facilities, but clearly students have access to them at home, too, not provided by the school, but by their parents.

Tampons are a little different, in that, unlike soap, which students might use at home, and then need in the school bathroom, a tampon or pad is typically used while in a hygienic spot, the bathroom at home, and then worn until it is removed, and only replaced in public when it's absolutely needed.
However they are replaced, in public, semi-routinely and women are likely to carry a supply with them in a variety of situations.
Menstruating female students are unlikely to come to school without a tampon and then suddenly need a pad or tampon during the day; they are likely to be carrying those supplies with them.
If for some reason they are not, a student should be able to simply ask to go to the bathroom, or school clinic, and a staff person should be able to provide her with a pad or tampon.
So, asking schools to provide students who might occasionally need a pad or tampon, is reasonable.

Asking them to constantly supply them with such items, is unreasonable, and would be akin to asking the school to continually provide students with toilet paper, soap and Band-Aids, to use whenever they needed them at home.

How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, it's a two way street when it comes to our screened devices.
In one way, we can argue that the screens we have everyday make our lives easier, more entertaining, and more productive.
On the other hand, too much screen usage makes our social interactions more limited and less meaningful.
So it is a delicate balance of how much is too much of the ever evolving digital world, and there isn't yet a standard for how much screen time is healthy.
In recent news, China has banned children under the age of 18 from playing online games.
Is this cruel and unfair?
Definitely.
But is this because of an over-abundance of screen time causing the addiction and consequently the behavioral issues that we see in our youth today?
It's also a possibility.
That's why it's always a two-fold and multi-faceted discussion when it comes to something that can become exponentially more influential, powerful and persuasive with time.

What I suggest is that parents, companies, and the government should step in and try to change the nature of our screen habits, before this new digital world starts overtaking the more traditional ways of life of our evolution.
The company, Facebook, has started removing the notifications feature on their home screen because of all the incessant distracting 'Likes' and '+1's'.
Google has also implemented the 'Do Not Disturb' feature to help you turn off your phone at night, if that's what you want to do.
However, these steps are just the initial steps and the companies need to do more to ensure that we aren't getting lost in our digital world.
China's banning of people under the age of 18 from playing games is an extreme and drastic step to take, and I wouldn't want to see this type of action taken in the United States.

Instead, a federal law to urge app makers and companies to monitor the screen habits of our youth might be more effective in preventing things like compulsive gambling, compulsive shopping, compulsive texting, and any type of addiction that leads to more unnecessary screen time.
Educators and parents should also step up to ensure our kids are not losing valuable time in their development, health, and social life because they are lost within the confines of their screens.
A more hands-on approach and a more sensitive level of mentorship for our youth can reduce the let-down from our digital world by introducing more hands-on experiences and personality.
If you are a parent, spending more time and having activities with your kid would help them spend less time on their phones.
To recap, I never want any banning or any drastic measures for people to limit their screen time.
It doesn't work and it will not deter people from not using their devices.
Instead, we should talk about the nuanced, more specific and technical aspects about how to balance the modern lifestyle with the ways of our ancestors.
This can be done by analyzing and studying different aspects of life like our social interaction, our health, and our cognitive ability, where all of these three aspects are intertwined.
Having devices with screens will not go anytime soon, but I just hope for the sake of our survival, devices will play a more positive role in our daily routines instead of the other way around.

In short, stereotypes are something that tends to be employed by bad writers.
However, this isn't necessarily the case with stereotypes found in some works that were created a long time ago.

These characters that have become hackneyed and stereotypical in modern use,  might have been fresh and new when they were first created, and even created by people who were trying to do something new and different, or be as accurate as possible in their portrayal of a group of people.
Human knowledge progresses, and as it does, so does our understanding of the world and the people in it.

So while a lot of the stereotypes that are considered most offensive now were created in works that were created a long time ago, they were created in an era when people didn't know as much about the world as we do now, and I'm more inclined to try to view those works from long ago in the context of the time in which they were created, rather than judge them by the standards of today.

two hours later, I awoke with a grand thirst and reached for my cold, water bottle on the bedside table.

Should College Athletes Be Paid?
Do you think college athletes should be paid?
Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?
What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?
In my opinion, this argument is a sound base, but is only half of the picture.
I think college athletes should be paid - they are essentially working for their schools, and should be compensated as other student workers are.
TThat said, te argument that paying college athletes would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni is a valid one.
Or rather, that it could hurt students, schools, etc.
It doesn't have to.
It would be complicated, but rules, limits, and regulations could be developed to prevent or solve most of the issues that would arise from paying student athletes.
It could be argued that it is inherently unfair - that some sports are more popular than others, and that some schools have more money than others.
Which is true.
But some schools already have more money than others, better teams than others, and have other advantages.
And the same with students - some are just better athletes and are highly courted already.
It seems unfair to take advantage of students talents and not compensate them.
Yes, certain athletes in popular sports will make more money, and certain schools will be more desirable than others.

But tht is post-school life anyway - graduates with degrees from 'better'  schools have an easier time finding better, higher paying jobs, and student athletes from schools with strong programs are more likely to go on to be professional athletes.

In fact, allowing college athletes to be paid, with oversight and a number of regulations, might help cut down on the unofficial and rather shady system of perks that is now used, making the whole system much more transparent and accountable.
More attention would be paid to what students are actually receiving, and with caps might actually be fairer to all students.
So, I believe there are a number of issues with paying student athletes, but there are also a lot of issues with the current system.
Paying athletes like any other employee would allow a more fair system that could be regulated and monitored, and withg teh right rules could benefit everyone.

What Stereotypical Characters Make You Cringe?
What stereotypical characters in books, movies or television shows make you cringe and why?

In my opinion, stereotypes that are portrayed in works of fiction are generally not intended to be harmful, and may come about unconsciously, but they do exacerbate feelings that lead to discrimination against, and sometimes direct harm to, marginalized groups in society.
For this reason, I would generally prefer not to watch or read something that revels in stereotypes, but sometimes I endure such things because of the cultural or entertainment value.
I suspect that if I was a member of a marginalized group, or was otherwise directly affected, I might take a stronger stance against such works.

I hrve already written at length about how I feel about stereotypes in general, so for today, I would like to talk about some of te most egregious instances of stereotyping in ymyreading or viewing experiences?.
Please note that in all cases, I am not claiming negligence on the part of the author.

I cannot know or predict what the author truly had in mind, but I will allow for the possibility (nay, the probability) that the author was simply relaying feelings that he or she had picked up from society.
The fact that society felt this way is not the author's fault, but I still take exception to the fact that the author reinforces these feelings.
So, onto the business at hand, the most common and harmful stereotype I see is that of black people.
This goes back to the Jim Crow era in which African-Americans were portrayed as happy fools who loved to work on plantations, where they could dance and sing in the sunlight.
Needless to say, this was never true, but it made white audiences feel better about themselves.
In this one case, I think that the stereotype was indeed created from willful malice.
Hattie McDaniels's character in Gone with the Wind is another example.
She is portrayed as someone who would be helpless if she was not enslaved by a rich white family, and we are meant to believe that she is grateful for what she received.
However, this is also an instance in which a black woman was humanized and portrayed fairly respectfully on screen, so I cannot totally object to it.
For a far more serious example, let us consider the trope of the 'black friend.'
This is often a character who is portrayed with no depth, and simply exists to make the main characters (who are almost always white) appear to be more tolerant and worldly.
A black friend simply exists to make the audience think that the white characters are more popular and universally appreciated.
At times, the black friend even ends up having some connection to the underworld, which the main characters can harmlessly exploit.
This is just as bad as explicitly claiming that all black people are involved in crime, because that is what the audience is led to believe.
The only possible situation in which I would tolerate a stereotype is if it were dportrayedby an obviously ignorant character ,win a fictional setting, ho could not be expected to know any better.
This might actually be beneficial for society, because audiences who came to see a heroic white cast, might end up learning a subtle lesson about questioning the stereotypes that pervade our society.
Unfortunately, I cannot readily think of an example in which I have seen this happen in fiction, and there have been far to many examples of harmful stereotypes.
I hope that the few examples which I had time to share were illustrative of the broader point.

In your opinion, is it  Why do you think so?

The history of civilization is the history of expanding the universe of rights-bearing sentient beings.
For a while, slaves did not have rights, then women had no rights, and now it is time to realize that animals should have rights as well.
There is no qualitative difference between the suffering of an animal or that of a human.
We have a moral duty to treat sentient beings with respect and to reduce their suffering.
This is not a proposition to be argued for, rather, it is a moral imperative which is axiomatic.
How can we work to reduce animal suffering?
We can insist that farm animals be treated humanely, or else become vegetarian.
We can also work to reduce the suffering of wild animals by supporting animal preserves and parks where animals are free to roam.
We can also work to reduce the suffering of animals in laboratories by supporting animal rights groups who work to improve the conditions of animals in laboratories.
We  can also be kind to animals in our daily lives.
We can stop kicking dogs, we can stop torturing cats, we can stop using animals for sport or entertainment.
We can stop eating meat, we can stop wearing fur, we can stop using animals for scientific research.
We can feed wild animals in times of extreme weather, and drive with care near animal crossings.
There are already ample organization to support human rights and needs.

But to draw a contrast between helping suffering animals versus humans is a false dichotomy.
We can help both.
And we should.

Is Listening to a Book Just as Good as Reading It?
Do you listen to audiobooks?
What are the benefits, in your opinion, of listening instead of reading?
Are there advantages to reading that cannot be gained by listening?
Which method do you prefer?
Why?
In my opinion, audiobooks are a very different experience than reading, with unique advantages and disadvantages.
I have listened to them on occasion, and they fill a different role in my life than reading does, and I can't see myself ever giving up either one.
One of the benefits of audiobooks is that they are a great way to consume books while doing something else.
You can work, drive, cook, exercise, do chores or any number of things while listening to a book.

Another advantage of audiobooks is that they are in many ways, easier and less effortful than reading, so they're a great way to continue consuming books when you don't have the time or energy to read.
Reading a book requires a certain level of concentration and focus, while an audiobook is as simple to do as clicking 'play.'
Audiobooks also offer the situational advantage of being read by a professional narrator, which can make the experience of listening to a book more enjoyable than reading it.
This of course depends on the skill of the narration, and whether or not you enjoy the narrator's voice.
One completely unique advantage of audiobooks, is that they can simulate the experience of being read a bedtime story, and give you the chance to be read off into a soothing night's rest.
On the other hand, books have several advantages of their own.
They provide a a much more immersive experience than audiobooks.
There's something about the act of reading a book, consciously, that can makes you feel like you're in the story, and that's something that audiobooks can't provide.
Books can be more vivid, and can provide a greater sense of depth and detail than audiobooks.
There are no limitations of the environment or pacing or the author's voice, and everything is created by the reader's imagination.
Books can also be read at one's own pace, which is impossible with audiobooks.
It can be very frustrating to be eagerly awaiting the next event in a book, and then have to wait for the narrator to finish a sentence, a paragraph, or a chapter.
In closing, audiobooks aren't a replacement for books, and they aren't really better or worse.
Instead, they're a different way of consuming books, and they fill a different role in one's life than reading does.
Overall they're an advantage, since they allow a lover of books to consume books in ways and in situations where reading might be difficult or impossible.
