How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time During the Pandemic?
The coronavirus pandemic ended the screen time debate: Screens won.
We all now find ourselves on our screens for school, for work and for connecting with family and friends during this time of social distancing and increased isolation.
But should we be worried about this excessive screen use right now?
Or should we finally get over it and embrace the benefits of our digital devices?
In my opinion, there is a real risk.
Just because society has shifted its focus to a more pressing issue, doesn't mean that we don't still have a screen time problem.
The real problem isn't the time that kids spend on their smart phones, tablets or computer screens.
The problem is what they do with that time.
We've watched them, through the pandemic, learn from virtual classrooms.
This is an example of good screen time.

We have also seen many children submerge into online gaming to an unhealthy level, as well as some other social networking applications that have created a diversion that leads to an unhealthy amount of time on a screen.
We saw with this pandemic and the way society responded that most parents did not have a sufficient amount of control over how their children could use their devices.
It is common today for kids to have access to their own screen, and many of them have built a simulated life on the networks.
These networks have digital stores, simulated cities that are part of multiplayer games, and have access to an online news station that keeps kids up with current events.
There is a lot of good there but, as with anything else, there can be such a thing as too much of a good thing.
It's time to begin talking about the opposite of screen time, which is life time.
Too many kids have been living through the pandemic in isolation.
They haven't had the opportunity to go out and build new, real world, relationships.
That has led to a lot more screen time than ever before.
The more that kids use their screen devices, the less time they have for human contact and interaction in the real world.
Since many of them have been stuck at home, if they don't get that interaction from immediate family they find that they can get it online.
Unfortunately, the need for physical interaction pressures anyone that doesn't have a lot of friends to begin craving more and more screen time.
It's an addiction, and it should be treated as such.
We don't encourage addicts to continue to use.
We shouldn't encourage kids using their devices for 18 hours of a 24 hour day to continue staring at the screen.

Humans have a natural need for human contact and all of us, kids and adults, need the real world interaction even-more during stressful times like thisI believe that the best thing we can do for our kids is to give them the interaction that they crave.
It can be difficult to find the energy to do that, after working all day, but it's more than worth the effort.
The real world is where life occurs.
We need to get our kids back into the real world.
The screen world can be a really fun place, and there's a lot to learn, but it's not so very different than any other addiction.
We need to offer an alternative and the best way to do that is to interact with them ourselves.
I encourage everyone who reads this article to spend some time with their kids today.
No phones and no computers allowed.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, the main reason why extreme sports can be defined as a sport is for the same reason any other sport.
It is exciting and gives the participants a sense of competition and amusement.
If there is no thrill or excitement, it might be considered a life-threatening activity rather than a sport.
Climbing for fun, without the fun, is hanging wires, excavating, or doing any other monotonous job.
Extreme outdoor pursuit activities such as mountain climbing and caving are the epitome of this.
The difficulties of the climb, whether rock-climbing or mountain-climbing, or otherwise,  can make it even more thrilling and exciting.
Exactly like other sports, the underlying reason why people participate in these activities is to have fun and challenge themselves.
The adrenaline (fear/anger/happiness) rush experienced by the climber or caver makes it an attractive and highly rewarding activity.
Many of these extreme sports also provide a sense of accomplishment, due mainly to the dangers faced in combination to the athleticism required.
All sports have risk.
Some people just prefer to increase the risk difficulty.
he extreme thrills and extreme dangers of outdoor activities are what make them both exciting and rewarding.
If you take away the thrills and dangers, these sports would lose their reason to exist.
Sports are competitive.
It is no question that almost all types of sports, including extreme outdoor pursuit athletes, are meant to compete with others.
The thrill and adrenaline rush of winning, or the agony and suffering of defeat endured by competitors, leads to a sense of newfound perseverance and strength.
Participating in these sports allows players to experience new feelings of excitement.
This makes the sport addictive and people want to perform better and better, or push the boundaries further and further.
Extreme sports are just that.
They are sports that follow all the criteria of regular sports: competition, personal athleticism, and risk, but do it to an extreme degree.
They are sports, but only for the bravest of the brave.

In my opinion, the primary difference between listening and reading is the level of interaction one has with the book.
When you read, you are the one creating the images in your head.
The pace is your own.
The descriptions, the tone, the characters' voices, all are part of your creation.
Your emotions and actions are very much your own.
You are both a reader and a participant in the story.
You decide how much, if at all, you interact with the characters and both their conversations and actions.
When you are listening to an audiobook, your level of interaction is very different.
Instead of creating the images for yourself, you are using the reader's voice and intonations to create a mental picture.
The mood, tone, inflections, and interpretation have already been done for you by the voice artist.
You are a listener, rather than a player.
The voice artist is the one creating a mental picture for you, taking away the ability to create your own.
There are some levels in which this can be good.
For instance, you may not be able to read because you are visually impaired and cannot see the words.
Or if you struggle with a short attention span or problems focusing, listening may work better for you.
Or perhaps you simply don't like reading, or it is just more convenient to listen.
One downside of listening is that you cannot speed up or slow down the voice artist's reading.
It is even possible that you might dislike the voice of the narrator, which makes it impossible to listen to.
Either way,   listening to a book can give you a similar experience of reading, and it is great for encouraging children to read.
In the end, whether you read or listen to a book, just make time for the one you love!

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, it is not selfish to engage in extreme sports, so long as the risk is only to one's self.
What is selfish is to inflict the risk on someone else, like your family, friends or even innocent bystanders.
However, this is extremely rare in the case of what I generally think of as 'extreme sports', and is perhaps much more common in more traditional team sports or, especially, in auto racing.

There is, of course, the question of whether or not this risk is acceptable, even in rare cases, but I would argue that spectators at auto races, and especially those who crowd around the dirt tracks at rally events, knowingly and willingly take on that risk.
IBack to the question at hand,  believe much of the danger is a result of what participants want from extreme sports.
Most of what I think of as extreme sports are a contest in which an individual pushes his or her own personal limits.
This could be on a skateboard in a stunt park, or on the side of a remote mountain.
In these cases, they are really only risking their own life and limb, and as long as they are prepared to pay the consequences, they should be allowed to do so.
However, it becomes selfish to the point of being dangerous when such risk forces others, who might not know better or be aware of the risks to pay some of the ultimate cost.
If an extreme athlete is uninsured, or has publicly provided health insurance, he or she is passing on the cost of any potential injury to the broader community.
You could make the case that even a fully-insured athlete is using hospital resources that might be better applied elsewhere, but I feel that this is not really salient.
If one were to take this position, we would have to consider children selfish every time they take a risk, and I am not willing to go that far.
It is the willful refusal (or inability) to pay for the consequences of one's actions that I consider to be selfish, and most extreme athletes do not engage in such conduct.
However, I am not willing to completely dismiss the notion that some sports are too dangerous to be considered sporting events at all.
One on one combat is a genre of sports that definitely comes close to, and sometimes crosses this line.

I would agree that athletes should be allowed to engage in boxing, wrestling, or other martial-arts contests that involve physical contact and serious risk of injury to themselves and to their counterpart, but only if they are fully aware of what they are doing.
Obviously, those under 18 or those who are not otherwise considered mentally-able to sign a contract should be barred from these sports for that reason.
And, of course, if someone chose to engage in combat sports without adequate ability to pay for potential injuries, I would consider that action to be selfish.
They are unduly burdening others in society for the sake of their own excitement.
So, ys, there are risks when engaging in extreme sports, but it is important to remember that there are risks in most sports.
and in most aspects of daily life.
I hope that my point has been clear, that others should be free to take these risks with their own bodies, and with the bodies of willing co-participants.
What would be selfish, would be forcing the risk of any kind of harm, including financial harm, on others who do not consent.
The true question, and the one that should be addressed in public policy, is how to stop this behavior from propagating among those who may not.
Should a group insurance pool be set up for extreme athletes?
This is a practical question that could benefit from further discussion, but for now, I think my point has been clear, and I thank you for reading.

What Stereotypical Characters Make You Cringe?
What stereotypical characters in books, movies or television shows make you cringe and why?
Would you ever not watch or read something because of its offensive portrayal of someone?
In my opinion, stereotypical characters in fiction are as old as fiction itself.

Fiction is intrinsically based on stereotypes and generalizations about people or situations, because it is a way of condensing life into some kind of literary, visual, or auditory shorthand that is much easier to consume for the reader.

Stereotypes are very much a part of this, because creating an archetype or an archetype package for a character is a quick way for readers to be able to define that character in their mind as a character representing a certain group or circumstances.
Without stereotypes, fiction can be very difficult to write, and too long-winded for readers to bother with.
Of course, this doesn't mean that using stereotypes is entirely acceptable.
Some stereotypes, such as dated racial or cultural ones , have grown so outdated through changing times that they're now universally viewed as offensive.

Examples of this are black characters once considered benign, and cheerful, like Stepin Fetchit, Aunt Jemima or Uncle Remus, who are now considered offensive racial stereotypes no one in their right mind would create.
Similar ones include characters once seen as heroic, like Tonto and the Lone Ranger, who are now seen as bigoted and politically incorrect.
This isn't because stereotyping in fiction is bad, though.
It's simply because of the way history, cultures and values change over time.
Many of today's stories, though they bend over backwards to be 'politically correct' and 'non-problematic' have stereotypes.

The 'bad father', the 'overworked single mother', the 'depressed woman with a cat', the 'female character who is more capable, smarter, and morally virtuous than any of the male characters' are all examples of modern stereotypes that are acceptable now, but will one day doubtless be viewed as offensive, dated, and in bad taste, to the same extent Uncle Remus is now.
So I personally, accept stereotypes in fiction, and would never turn down or run from a book or a film because of its presence.
I try to see beyond the stereotype.
to the universal story that the writer is attempting to tell, and encourage other readers and viewers to approach stereotypes in fiction in a similar manner.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, extreme mountain climbing is a sport that is too dangerous for people to participate in.
I recently heard about an extreme mountain climber who died of his injuries after successfully climbing Mt.
Everest.
He had an altitude sickness that rendered him disoriented and unconscious.
And on top of that he was going blind from cerebral oedema, which resulted from a fall he had suffered shortly after his successful climb of Everest.
It was quite a scary story to learn about.

Upon reading that article, I really felt sympathetic for this man's family because I could only imagine the pain and suffering he must have been enduring as he was losing his sight and crumbling from altitude sickness.
I looked up his wife's Instagram account after he passed and it was clear that the family was devastated at the loss.
She was obviously coping very hard.
One of the most gut-wrenching things that I read from her was that she couldn't bring herself to watch the video of her husband's last climb.
She had posted a picture of the video with the caption, 'Never mind, I can't watch it.
It's too painful.'
And yet he had done this climb knowing very well that it was dangerous and he might not make it back alive.
This made me feel angry because he was clearly putting his family through unnecessary torture, if it came to that.
And he was perfectly willing to do so even though he had a wife and three children.
When I saw that she had posted Instagram stories about taking her kids to his grave, I felt even more angry.
Her three children were all too young to be left without a father.
And now he's left her to deal with his death along with all the burdens of being a single mother.
Quite frankly, his recklessness with his life and that of his family's is a form of selfishness.
So I don't think that society should condone that kind of recklessness.

If I were to draw a legal distinction between what I consider dangerous versus what is dangerous enough to constitute a ban on an activity, I would use examples from the United States Code.

Should College Athletes Be Paid?
Do you think college athletes should be paid?
Or is a college scholarship and other non-monetary perks like the opportunity to play in front of cheering fans enough?

In 'Paying Students to Play Would Ruin College Sports,' Cody J. McDavis writes: 'Paying student-athletes might sound like a fairer way to treat students who generate so much money and attention for their colleges (not to mention the television networks that broadcast their games).
But paying athletes would distort the economics of college sports in a way that would hurt the broader community of student-athletes, universities, fans and alumni.
A handful of big sports programs would pay top dollar for a select few athletes, while almost every other college would get caught up in a bidding war it couldn't afford.'
Do you find his argument persuasive?
What possible difficulties or downsides might there be in providing monetary compensation to players?
In my opinion, paying student-athletes would not ruin college sports, at least not anymore than it has been ruined.
The NCAA is a business, and the players are the product.
College leagues are supposed to be amateur, but the NCAA is a billion dollar business.
It functions as a recruitment organization for the NFL and NBA, and has done this for years, and it is a money-making machine.
Paying student-athletes would merely be a way to pay the people going through the long, minor-league, recruitment and training process.
That is, it would be a way to pay the people who are engaged in a process that amounts to a very long hiring selection period.
It's not just the leagues, and how they function as a recruitment organization for the pros, though.
It's also the college teams themselves.
College sports make schools tons of money.
Tickets to college games are expensive, and the schools make a lot of money from selling tickets.
Some of these tickets are as highly demanded as the tickets to the Super Bowl.
Also, the teams indirectly bring in a lot of money through merchandise, and the sale of TV rights, and through the alumni donations that are often tied to the success of the team.
It might be fair to say that at colleges with very good professional teams, the school itself, and the education it provides, are secondary to the sports team.

They're kind of a parasitic entity that sponges off the revenue generated by the team (among other sources), and it's only right that the players, who are in fact, supporting the school, should get a piece of the pie.
It's not unfair to say that college sports shouldn't be a business.
It's not unfair to say there's too much emphasis on them, and that they're more important to the schools than they  should be, and that education is being sacrificed for the sake of sports.
It's reasonable to argue that all of this should change, and that college sports should be more about education, and less about money.
But it's unreasonable to punish the players, who are the workers supporting this entire business model.

Perhaps college sports should be separated from the rest of the college experience, but until they are, student-athletes are merely the workers in a business that makes a lot of money, and they should be paid accordingly.

'Did you call me Majesty?
', I said to the bee.

I told the bee that my mother had always told me that I had a deadly allergy to bees, so I lived in fear of bees.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, i do not find it selfish to puruse risky sports like extreme mountain climbing.
Even though they may seem dangerous, i think everyone has their reasons for doing them.
Some people need that level of extreme to feel calm and peaceful in their mind, and without it they may not be the same type of person as they are with it.
Something like mountain climbing, so dangerous that your life is on the line requires a certain level of attention that just wipes out the rest of your stressors in your head.
Some people are naturally more stressed than other people and to them a coping strategy may be something like the dangerous sport of mountain climbing.
So to me, it is not selfish to participate in any risky sport.
It does depend on the reason you are doing it of course, but I dont think it is our decision to decide whether someone's reason is selfish or not.
This is something that is for them to decide.
I can personally relate to this state of mind because i need exercise and sports myself to calm my mind.
There is something about that extreme focus that is just very therapeutic to me in general.
I played football all my life, and this gave me something to focus on from the time i was eight years old, to the time i was 22.
Right after playing i needed to find that something that gave me the same feeling, or identity.
For this reason i got into boxing.
Boxing was the only thing that could give me that same feeling.
I needed that extreme focus to be able to function in my daily life.
I started to realize that being in my own head and being stressed was 1000 times worse than anything that could happen in that boxing ring.
I was never afraid of getting hurt in any sport, i was simply afraid of being in my own head.
I would do anything just not to be in my own head.
So i definitely get the person that is doing mountain climbing for peace of mind and for that adrenaline rush that some of us so desperately need.
That rush that we can not get outside of the sport.
I think that is why we do it.
I think that is why we do anything, for that positive feeling or consequence.
Doing it in that way is not selfish at all, it is selfless.
So in conclusion, i truly believe that it is not selfish to pursue risky sports as long as it is done for the right reason.

Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?
In your opinion, are we being bad citizens if we don't keep up with the news?
Do you think all people have some responsibility to know what is going on in the world?
Does engaging with current events actually do anything at all?
Why do you think the way you do?
In my opinion, we only have an obligation to keep up with the news, if it is relevant to us.

That is, if you are in a position where you can profit off of or effect real change with information, you have an obligation to know what is going on to the extent that that knowledge, will help you do those things.
f you are a CEO, you have an obligation to know what is going on in the world.
of business, and in the broader scheme of things that might affect your business.
If you are a doctor, you have an obligation to know what is going on in the world of medicine.
If you are a farmer, you have an obligation to know what is going on in the world of agriculture.
If you are an actor or writer or singer, you have an obligation to know what is going on in the world of entertainment.
What then if you're an ordinary citizen?
Well, then you have an obligation to know what is going on in the world that might affect you or that of people who might be close to you.
If you have children, for example, you have an obligation to know about what's going on in the realm of schooling, so you can properly choose how to educate your children.
You also need to know about changes in the law that affect education.
You need to know about health crises that your children might be impacted by.

Of course, that goes beyond parenting, you also need to know about those things if you have a frail elderly person in your life, or an ailing cousin, or a sibling who cannot take care of themselves, and even for yourself.
If you work, you need to know about changes in the economy that may impact your job, or political issues to the extent that they could impact the economy.
If you pay taxes , you have an obligation to know about legislation that impacts taxes.
If you're a homeowner, you need to know about housing and mortgage issues, and developments related to home maintenance.
If you are a tenant, you need to know about rent issues, and if you live in subsidized housing, the happenings in the housing industry also.
If you're a professional, you need to know about developments in your field to learn new information in order to improve upon your ability to operate  within it.
I think it's fair to say that engaging with current events can definitely impact your life and the lives of those around you in meaningful way.
I can think of many examples from my own life, for instance it's been raining unseasonable amounts here of late, and I prevented cycling into a flood by watching the weather news yesterday.
I don't think then, that this is an obligation; it is merely enlightened self-interest.

Should schools step in to help?
Should schools be required to provide free pads and tampons to students?
How are pads and tampons similar to toilet paper, soap, Band-Aids and other products that are already provided in schools?
How are they different?
While I have not personally experienced period shaming or period poverty, I have witnessed such incidents first hand when I attended high school, and middle school as well.
I think it is a negative outcome for female students, that personally affects them psychologically, and for a long period of time.
Ideally , girls should be able to buy and receive whatever products they might need for their menstruation without any worry.
Schools should step in and help this natural process of life that female students go through.
For many students, it can be a daunting endeavor to understand the process of which pads or tampons to buy.
For others, poverty can affect whether they can buy menstrual process on a constant and regular basis.
Thus, providing free pads and tampons can help limit the period shaming, and period poverty that female students are regularly subject to.
Tampons and Pads are much similar to Band-Aids and similar items provided by the school.
For example, they are hygienic items like soap and toilet paper, intended to make the user clean and avoid appearing unhygienic.
Like Band-Aids, they stop bleeding for a period of time and as long as one continues to wear them, and they have to be changed out every while.
I am sure that students would appreciate seeing them in the school, just as they would any other supply readily available in school.
However, unlike Band-Aids and other items, their ought to be a better sense of privacy for the students requesting tampons and pads.

For example, there should not be any announcement in an auditorium or over the intercom that the student need pads or tampons, and ideally the school would not keep a record of such, allowing the students to remain anonymous when requesting the pads and receiving them.
Through that, they can receive the tampons and pads they require, without feeling judged for doing so and potentially being stigmatized for what is effectively a natural and commonplace occurrence.
Schools ought to be a place where students feel comfortable and able to learn and develop as individuals.
Providing tampons and pads are a critically way for schools to do so for female students.

By offering them in a private and respectful way, schools can give comfort and stability for students undergoing their period, that otherwise might be judged and ridiculed for lacking access to such supplies.

Is It Wrong to Focus on Animal Welfare When Humans Are Suffering?
Would you be surprised to hear that a study found that research subjects were more upset by stories of a dog beaten by a baseball bat than of an adult similarly beaten?

The amount of cruelty in the world is staggering.
Many millions of living things, human and animal, are made to suffer at the hands of others daily.

It makes no sense to say that harm to animals is less important than harm to people, because there is no way to find a characteristic of people that makes them more important in a moral calculus than animals.
What morally-relevant characteristic do humans have that animals don't?
Intelligence?
No, because some animals are smarter than some humans (e.g., a a chimp has more intelligence than a newborn baby).
Self-awareness?
Animals are self aware.
Ability to know right from wrong?
Many experiments show a moral sense in some animal species.
The list goes on.
There is really no morally-relevant characteristic that decides what is more important: human or animal suffering.
That means all harm to all living things is morally relevant.
And people should care about both.
It's not that it is wrong to focus on animal welfare when humans are suffering.
It's that there cannot to a moral defense of such a view that is neither circular nor specious.
It must simply be a matter of personal preference -- and that is okay.
Some will be more moved by animal suffering than human, and vice-versa.
What is important is that we fight to end needless suffering, whether the victims are human or animal.

Is Listening to a Book Just as Good as Reading It?
Do you listen to audiobooks?

Are there advantages to reading that cannot be gained by listening?
Which method do you prefer?
Why?
In my opinion, audiobooks are not a sufficient replacement for real books.
I don't listen to audiobooks because I consider myself to be a visual learner, and while I suppose that good audiobook narrators aim to cater to me, it's just not the same for me.
I really have to be seeing it in my mind's eye if I'm to get the full effect of a story.
If I'm just listening to someone read it, I don't feel one bit of emotion or connection with the characters.
And moreover, it's just that much easier for me to 'switch off' when listening to someone else read - particularly if what I'm listening to isn't capturing my attention.
Oftentimes, when I'm listening to an audiobook, I'll find myself daydreaming about times I'd rather forget, or something bad that happened today, or my looming deadlines...
I just can't concentrate fully on what I'm listening to if my mind is wandering.
This isn't to say that audiobooks can't be tremendously useful, and I do use them occasionally.
I mean, if I'm driving, I can't even pretend that it isn't ten times safer for me to be listening to someone else read instead of trying to read myself.

On my commute to and from school, I often find that listening to John Scalzi narrate his own audiobooks is enjoyable - even though I don't think I get as much out of the audiobooks as I do from reading them my own.

Sometimes, listening to the audiobook version of my science textbook is sufficient to recall the information I need for an exam - although I will caveat that it is not sufficient to really understand it.
So I'm not in any way trying to demonize audiobooks by saying that I don't use them.
I definitely do.
I just think it's important to point out that I really don't enjoy listening to them much because it isn't the same as reading a real book.
Reading a real book really helps me to get invested in the story and characters.
And I always find that I 'm more easily able to form a real, deep connection to the characters of what I'm reading if I can see them and visually connect to their words.
Usually when I read, my mind is actively visualizing the book's imagery, which I find is something that can't quite be replicated when listening to someone else read it to me.

I've had some friends tell me that they really enjoy audiobooks in part because they can make up their own interpretation of the story when they aren't seeing it played out the way the author intended on the page.
I can understand this viewpoint, but I don't find much value in it.
After all, couldn't I just retort that people don't really know it could have been intended any other way?
And who's to say that an audiobook vocalist doesn't force his or her own views of a book or plotline on their listeners?
I have never felt that I couldn't make up my own interpretation of an author's ending in a book that I had in my hands.
So my friends' perspective seems very skewed to me.
It could just be their bias, though, because I know how much they enjoy hearing audiobooks on the regular.
In conclusion, I am happy to stick to reading real books.
I think that there's a lot to be said for the real, tangible relationship between a reader and their pages.
Plus, there's definitely a lot to be said for the tactile experience that a real book allows - that's a whole other argument for another day.

Is It Wrong to Focus on Animal Welfare When Humans Are Suffering?
Would you be surprised to hear that a study found that research subjects were more upset by stories of a dog beaten by a baseball bat than of an adult similarly beaten?
Or that other researchers found that if forced to choose, 40 percent of people would save their pet dog over a foreign tourist.
Why do you think many people are more empathetic toward the suffering of animals than that of people?
In your opinion, is it wrong to focus on animal welfare when humans are suffering?
Why do you think so?

In my opinion, I think that people tend to be more concerned about individual cases, whether human or animal, more so than statistics, so I am not surprised to hear that research subjects were more upset about the idea of a dog being beaten than the idea of a human being similarly beaten.

It is a simple fact that people are somewhat inured to violence against humans because we see so much of it in the media, and yet violence against charismatic animals such as dogs or seals is both shocking and upsetting to us.
We have to remember that this result came from a laboratory.
If people were in a real situation in which they could either stop an unfamiliar dog from being beaten, or a stranger from being beaten, I doubt that anyone would choose the dog.
I tdo not hink that iitwis rong to focus on animal welfare when humans are suffering, bsimply because the former grabs our attention more acutely.
Bt I do think that we need to be careful not make decisions that have real-world consequences using only our feelings, rather than our rational thoughts.

For example, we might oppose the hunting of whales, yet if a small community of indigenous people are only able to survive through the winter by sustainably killing one whale per year for meat and blubber, then we should not let our idealistic view of noble, graceful animals distract from the needs of real, living persons.
As for the other question of people preferring to save their own dog, rather than the life of a foreign tourist, I cannot really judge anyone too harshly.
How many of us could truly say that we would prefer to save a stranger over a family member?
Wouldn't you prefer to save your estranged uncle even if it meant allowing two or more other people to die as a result?
People are close to their pets, and treat them as family, so it is not surprising, or unethical, for us to prioritize their welfare.
My main objection is treating the vague idea of an animal as more valuable than the real-world welfare of a human.
This, of course, leads to more philosophical questions, and ones that I cannot give a confident answer to.
For example, is it wrong to eat meat?
Humans benefit from the nutritional density of meat, but animals are obviously harmed.
I think that this is a personal choice that each individual should make, and one that they shouldn't make lightly.
As long as they are aware of the fact that animals suffer for their convenience, then (with some serious regulations in place to prevent extreme suffering) they should be allowed to do so.
Likewise, I tend to favor animal research for medical purposes, because ultimately, a lot more suffering is prevented than is caused.
But, of course, I accept that this is not always a utilitarian calculation.
Some may feel that it is wrong to deliberately harm an animal or a human, and I respect that opinion.
In so many words, I can understand why people tend to favor the lives of highly-visible animals over the lives of unseen humans, but I do have to strenuously object.
The needs of the many, as it were, far outweigh the needs of the few.
A woman has been dating guy after guy, but it never seems to work out.
She's unaware that she's actually been dating the same guy over and over; a shapeshifter who's fallen for her, and is certain he's going to get it right this time.
One day, she finds out the truth.
It was quite disconcerting.
She was sitting on her living room sofa with her boyfriend, Ted watching a movie and eating popcorn.
Ted was holding the bowl.
She turned to say something to him, and instead of the blonde haired, blue eyed, light complected man of average height she was dating, there sat a tall, dark haired man with a closely cropped beard.
He was wearing the same clothes as Ted.
He was holding the popcorn bowl like Ted, but he didn't look anything like Ted.
She hopped up off the sofa.
This couldn't be Ted, but at the same time it couldn't NOT be Ted.
She had been sitting next to this man the whole time.
'Sue,' he said in a voice quite different than Ted's, 'what's wrong?'
She pointed at him with a trembling finger.
He looked down and realization dawned across his handsome face.
'Sue,' he said.
'Don't be afraid.
It's me.
I know I look different than I did a moment ago, but I'm still the same person that you've been dating for the past two months and the same person who sat down on the sofa an hour ago.
I admit, I look different, but it's still me.'
She looked at him, then at the popcorn bowl, then back at him.
'I don't understand,' she said.
He took a deep breath and motioned for her to sit back down.
'I'll tell you,' he said.
He went on to explain that he was born a shapeshifter, like his father had been.
As a child, it was hard for his parents to keep track of him.
He couldn't go to school, because when he was little, he didn't fully understand that not everyone had the same ability as he did.
Once he was old enough to understand, he didn't always have control over when he shifted.
By the time he was a teenager, he had good control but on rare occasions, it would happen unexpectedly, like it had tonight.
Sue seemed shocked but given what she had just seen, she knew that Ted was telling the truth.
She'd seen it with her own eyes.
Seeing that she was accepting what he had told her, Ted went on.
'First, my real name is Kyle Wilkerson.
The reason I didn't tell you my real name is because I have loved you for many years and dated you four times before and it didn't work out.
I was Liam, Joe, Henry and Bob before we met while I was calling myself Ted.
I'm really sorry, but I wanted to be with you so badly that I kept trying.'
ue was stunned.
She had dated this man four times before?
She thought back and realized that each of those men after Liam had seemed to know her better than the one before.
Now she realized it was because each one DID know her better, as they had spent time together.
Ted looked anxious as Sue sat in thought.
Finally she told him that she was touched that he wanted to be with her so badly that he kept trying over and over again, but that for now she needed him to leave so she could think things through.
Ted, or actually Kyle, stood up.
'Also,' she said, 'what is your true form?'
He explained that he didn't know, because he had changed so often that he didn't really know what he looked like.
'What form do you feel most comfortable in?'
Before her eyes, he shrunk a couple of inches.
His hair stayed dark brown, but some light highlights appeared as it grew near shoulder length.
His nose got a little longer, his eyes changed to an emerald green.
He was stunning to look at.
'I am going to think about what I should do,' Sue said.
'But if I see you again, I want you to be in this shape, because this shape is what you are most comfortable in.'
Kyle smiled at her as he walked out the door.
She closed it behind him and leaned against it.
She had a lot to think about.
She went to bed that night and slept fitfully.
She thought it was unlikely she'd ever find a man that wanted to be with her so badly.
A few days later she called him and they met for coffee.
He looked like the person he'd last shifted into, and she told him that she was willing to start over and see where it went.
They eventually married and had three children.
Sue now understood what Kyle's mother went through, as one of the three was a shapeshifter, too.
She had realized that might be the case so she was prepared, but little Ted was definitely more of a handful than his two non-shapeshifting siblings.
But she loved him as much as the others and never regretted marrying Kyle and having his children.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, some sports like extreme mountain climbing are definitely too dangerous to be called a sport.
I know this from personal experience, which is really unfortunate.
I have had two friends die in the mountains.
The two friends who died are named Soeurette and Matt.
Soeurette was a friend of mine from high school.
We went to Ridgewood High School together in New Jersey.
She was a year older than me, and she started dabbling in mountain climbing during college, since she studied abroad in Southeast Asia for a semester where there were abundant mountains.
Meanwhile, Matt was a friend that I met through Soeurette.
Soeurette and Matt met at a bar some time after college and became a couple.
They eventually got engaged.
Soeurette convinced Matt to try mountain climbing with her.
This was a big mistake.
Matt had always had somewhat of a thrill-seeking nature and was a bit of a daredevil, but he had never done anything like mountain climbing before.
So he was all for trying it.
Soeurette and Matt went to the Alps in France to try mountain climbing.
Unfortunately, they were not prepared for the conditions they encountered.
It was just days before their wedding, and they were trying to get in one last adventure together before settling down.
The two of them were on a mountain called the Aiguille du Midi, which is a popular mountain for mountain climbers.
It is a very tall mountain, and it is very steep.
It is considered to be a difficult mountain to climb.
Soeurette and Matt were climbing the mountain together, but they were not roped together.
This decision proved to be fatal.
They were climbing the mountain, and they were about halfway up when Matt slipped.
He fell about 1000 feet down the mountain.
Soeurette tried to grab him, but she was not able to.
She fell down the mountain after him.
She was not able to stop herself from falling, and she fell all the way to the bottom of the mountain.
She died on impact, as did Matt.
I was devastated when I heard about this.
I had known Soeurette for a long time, and I had been friends with her for years.
I was also friends with Matt, and I had known him for years as well.
I was shocked when I heard about their deaths because I had never thought that they would die in the mountains.
I thought that they were experienced enough to know what they were doing.
But now I know that mountain climbing is a dangerous sport, and it can be fatal even for experienced mountain climbers.
So today, I do not climb mountains anymore.
I have not climbed a mountain since Soeurette and Matt died.
Because of the loss of my two friends, I now take the position that extreme mountain climbing is too dangerous to be called a sport.
We shouldn't condone the sport, and we shouldn't encourage people to do it.
The distinction between a sport and an extreme sport is that a sport is something that you can do safely.
And for any sport that you cannot participate in safely, we should get rid of it as a sport altogether.
It's in the best interests of society and athletes to do so.
For extreme mountain climbing, you cannot do it safely.
In fact, people love the thrill of mountain climbing because it is dangerous.
That's what led Matt to try mountain climbing in the first place.
I hope that people will realize that sports like mountain climbing are too dangerous to be called sports and that people will refrain from participating in them.

I mean, that's a lot of money!
That's especially the case considering that the average woman spends a huge amount of money on tampons and pads over her lifetime.
Let's break down those numbers for a minute.
The average woman menstruates for about 30 years.
Now, a box of tampons costs $7 and a box of pads costs $5.
But wait, now we need to figure out how many boxes a woman goes through in a year.
If a woman goes through 14 boxes of pads and tampons in a year, that's $2,940.
And then we need to multiply that by 30 years.
I cannot fathom how much money I would have saved if I didn't have to worry about how I was going to afford tampons and pads.

If a girl tried to use toilet paper as a pad, it would just fall apart.
It would immediately soak through and leave a girl's underwear and pants completely soaked.
And if a girl tried to use toilet paper as a tampon, it would just fall out.
And that would be a huge mess, and would cause a lot of pain and embarrassment.
So no, toilet paper is not an adequate substitute for pads and tampons.
And a man should not speak when he has no idea what it's like to menstruate.

It's really a small price to pay for a girl's dignity and for a girl's future financial freedom and security.
For these reasons, I humbly request school districts across the country to consider the arguments made herein and provide free pads and tampons to their students.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, existing sports are already too dangerous.

Assuming that we don't want to get into the business of banning sports that have been around for years, I think it's reasonable to use the most dangerous existing sports, as an upper limit on what is acceptable.
The question then becomes, what is the most dangerous sport?
The likely answer is some kind of combat sport, like boxing, mixed martial arts, or wrestling.
The athletes who compete in those sports are risking serious injury and even death, each and every time they step into the ring or onto the mat.
Exactly how high the risk is, could be calculated by looking at the number of deaths and serious injuries per year, and the number of participants.
So, this number would be the upper limit for acceptable risk in a particular sport.
It follows that when a new sport is introduced, it should be compared to this upper limit, and if it is more dangerous in terms of injuries or deaths, it should be banned.
This could be tricky; for example, in boxing, the risk of death is relatively low, but the risk of brain damage is high.
Other dangerous sports reverse this trend.
Some regulatory agency would have to be created to make these kinds of comparisons between sports, and to decide which ones are too dangerous to be allowed.
Of course, a new sport might not have detailed records of injuries and deaths, so it would be necessary to estimate the risk.
If deemed too high, the organization that created the sport would have to make changes to reduce the risk, or else competition in it would be prohibited.
Once a sport is established, records would have to be kept of injuries and deaths, so that the risk could be calculated.
A sport that exceeds the threshold, would be required to make changes to reduce the risk, or else it would be banned.
This would apply to existing sports, as well as new ones.
Sports are an inherently dangerous activity, and there is no way to eliminate all risk.
However, it seems absurd to attempt to ban all dangerous sports, as some people have suggested, because this would begin a disturbing trend of government interference in our lives.
The best approach is a rational, common-sense, empirical one, aiming to set a reasonable limit on the acceptable level of risk, and then to require that all sports stay below that level.
This will balance the desire for personal liberty, with the need to protect the safety of the participants.

All of those activities are statistically more likely to cause harm to the person doing it but no one would consider any of those activities as selfish.
I think that it is a personal decision to partake in these activities., just like partaking in any activity is.

Is Listening to a Book Just as Good as Reading It?
Do you listen to audiobooks?
What are the benefits, in your opinion, of listening instead of reading?
Are there advantages to reading that cannot be gained by listening?
Which method do you prefer?
Why?
The utility of audiobooks depends upon whether one is listening to fiction or nonfiction.
For nonfiction books, listening is a fully functional way of absorbing the material.
For fiction, however, listening is a poor substitute for reading.
The reason for this is that the experience of reading a book is not just about absorbing the information., but to read good fiction is to inhabit another world.
I think that listening to a book is a good way to get the gist of the material, but it is not a good way to experience the book as a lived reality.
The reader is transported to the world of the book, and the reader is able to experience that world in a way that is not possible by just listening to a narration.
In an audiobook the reading experience is necessarily a mediated one.
The narrator supplies pacing, emphasis, even accents.
The narrator is the voice of the book, and the reader is not.
I think that the narrator's view of the material is valid and important--for them, not necessarily for me.
I don't want to hear the narrator's voice, I want to hear the author's.
Reading a book is an activity that is both creative (supplying our own history and interpretation) and collaborative.
But that essential collaboration is with the author--and only with the author.
Think about the last time you read--really read-- a book.
For me, it was Stephen King's Dark Tower series, thousands of pages over eight novels.
Picking up that story was pleasant because I was entering another world.
I did listen to parts if that audiobook, and was underwhelmed because the voice of the narrator was not the voice I had heard in my head.

In closing,  think that the experience of reading a book is a fundamentally different experience than listening to an audiobook., because it is fundamentally an act of co-creation, and not merely the ingestion of facts
What Are the Most Important Things Students Should Learn in School?
In your opinion, what are the most important things students should learn in school?
What is the most important thing you have learned in school?
How has this knowledge affected your life?
How do you think it will help your success in the future?
In my opinion, students should learn skills that will improve their ability to work in the real world.
That is, school should emphasize vocational education.
In addition to this, school should have a secondary emphasis on basic education, such as reading and writing, mathematics, foreign languages, and history.
As it stands now, students leave school not only without marketable skills, but many of them are also functionally illiterate and innumerate.
They also lack a grasp of their own nation's history and the events that have taken place in the world.
These are the things schools, *should* be responsible for teaching.

In reality, schools end up spending so much time and energy on non-essential subjects, such as liberal arts, multicultural education, and teaching the 'correct' way to think about political issues, that they seldom teach students how to succeed in work and life.

Students also spend so much time thinking about their social life and worrying about their personal safety, rather than actually trying to learn, that they are too distracted and demoralized to learn very much of whatever their teachers arbitrarily decide to emphasize.
I base this on my observations of the young, who I believe are getting a worse education than I did as a member of the previous generation, but also my own experiences.
As it turns out, I learned very little in school in the conventional sense.
My parents taught me to read and write; friends taught me how to do math;  and I spent copious amounts of time in the library and with our Encyclopedia Britannica, learning about history.
Much of what I did learn in school, involved dubious socialization, self-defense, and wrong-headed political opinions, all of which were 'learning' that I could have done without.
So I'd like to spare other students the same useless and even counter-productive 'education' that I had to endure.

Schools should be safe places that students can go to learn essential job skills and basic knowledge,  not places where they're targets of criminality, indoctrinated, and taught to hate and fear others.
Sadly I fear,  the latter is more likely than the former, and far from improving from my days in public school, it's actually getting worse.

Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
Some sports, like extreme mountain climbing, are dangerous.

Since there are varying degrees of risk in most, if not all, sports (such as the possibility of concussions, broken bones and even death), how does one decide where the line might be drawn between what is reasonable and what is not?
Are some sports simply too dangerous to be called a sport?
In my opinion, there are activities that put an undue burden on the community.
Playing football, baseball, hockey or other team sports is relatively low risk, and tend to be good for a community.
Those sports give people something do do, whether as spectators or as participants.
Other sports are more of a daring pursuit, where an individual, or group of individuals, test some extreme element and put themselves at great risk.
They also run the risk of becoming a burden to society.
They may fill a hospital bed that would be needed by someone else, or they may require expensive emergency transport, that they cannot afford.
The cost of their injuries fall not only on them, but on us.
In order to keep those kinds of sports going, we, as a society would have to subsidize them.
These activities may have some value as spectator sports, but that value is outweighed if there are a large number of injuries, or even deaths, that occur as a result of their practice.
Although the desire to promote or practice these sports may be an individual decision, society has a responsibility to regulate them.
It is our infrastructure that is put to the test when something goes wrong.
Communities to not sacrifice resources to build hospitals, roads and emergency systems for this purpose.
The cost falls on all of us.
Personal freedom is important, and most would agree that it is central to American life.
The problem arises when a person's individual liberty, and the extent to which they exploit their freedom, begins to drain community resources.
In other words, when the ability to pursue a chosen lifestyle causes a drain on the system that depends on it to function, society can impose its interests.
Society has a duty to do so.
Personal freedom has limits and those limits can be derived in a fair and democratic way.
That is why we vote.
We vote with the interest of the community, as a whole, in mind.
That is the only responsible way to make those choices.
Otherwise, there is no limit to the freedom an individual might want to claim.
They may claim that they can choose to hurt other people, however indirectly, in pursuit of their own goals.
That is wrong.
It is not a meaningful expression of freedom.
That is an attack on the institutions that allow us to live freely.
Extreme sports need to be analyzed and dispositioned by the community, as a whole.
That is the only fair way to evaluate them, and to decide on regulations that will govern them.
